Filial Piety
FIL-ee-ul PY-ih-tee
n. phrase (biblical ethics; fifth commandment)
From Latin filialis (of a son or daughter; from filius, son) + pietas (dutifulness, reverence, proper devotion); in Roman thought, the foundational virtue of right relation to gods, parents, and country — reoriented by Scripture toward the one true God and His ordered family.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Filial piety is the reverent honor, obedience, and care that children owe to their parents — a duty rooted not in culture or sentiment but in the law of God. The fifth commandment stands at the head of the second table of the Decalogue: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long upon the land which the LORD your God is giving you” (Ex 20:12). The connection of honor to long life in the land is not incidental; it links the stability of the covenant family to the stability of the covenant nation. When families unravel — when parents are dishonored, abandoned, or despised — the social fabric woven by God begins to tear. Paul cites the fifth commandment in the New Testament as the “first commandment with a promise” (Eph 6:2), demonstrating its perpetual moral force beyond the Mosaic economy. The command is directed to children in the Lord — Christ's people of every age — not merely to minors. Adult children continue to owe honor, provision, and care to aging parents; the widows left without family support in 1 Timothy 5:4, 8 illustrate what filial piety looks like when parents are old and dependent. Proverbs holds both sides: “Listen to your father who begot you, and do not despise your mother when she is old” (Prov 23:22). The honor is not contingent on the parents' perfection — it is due to the office and to the God who placed one in that family. The 1689 LBCF (19.5) includes the fifth commandment as part of the perpetually binding moral law, applicable to all persons in all ages.

Webster 1828 Definition

The reverent honor, obedience, and care that children owe their parents — commanded as the fifth of the Ten Commandments with a promise attached, grounding family order in the law of God and the covenant stability of society. Distinct from piety generally: filial piety is the specific fifth-commandment duty of children toward parents.

FILIAL PIETY, n. phrase. From Latin filialis (of a child) + pietas (dutiful reverence); the divinely commanded honor, obedience, and care that children — of any age — owe to their parents.

The fifth commandment is the first of the second table, governing human-to-human duties. Its placement suggests that right relation to parents is the gateway to right relation to all human authority — magistrate, elder, husband, employer — and that the dishonoring of parents is not a private family matter but a public sin with covenantal consequences.

The commandment covers more than obedience in childhood. It encompasses reverence (treating parents with dignity and respect), obedience (following parental direction while under their authority), provision (caring for aging parents materially), and honor (speaking of parents with gratitude, not contempt).

Paul's “first commandment with a promise” (Eph 6:2) signals that the fifth commandment operates on a typological as well as a moral level: the son or daughter who honors parents images the Son who honored the Father and thereby stands in the inheritance.

Modern cultures in which the elderly are warehoused, the authority of parents is eroded by the state or popular culture, and adult children feel no obligation to aging fathers and mothers are cultures in acute fifth-commandment failure, whatever they may confess.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:12 — "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long upon the land which the LORD your God is giving you."

Ephesians 6:1 — "Children, obey your parents in the Lord — for this is right."

Ephesians 6:2 — "“Honor your father and mother” — which is the first commandment with a promise —"

Proverbs 23:22 — "Listen to your father who begot you, and do not despise your mother when she is old."

Modern Corruption

Modern individualism severs the child from obligation to the parent; the therapeutic movement reframes filial duty as potentially harmful attachment; the progressive state substitutes its own authority for parental authority — all representing fifth-commandment failure.

expand to see more

The most powerful modern corruption of filial piety is the therapeutic re-framing of parental authority as potentially causing suffering. Therapeutic culture teaches that the adult child's primary obligation is to her own wellbeing and personal authenticity — that parents who imposed structure, discipline, or a particular worldview may have caused harm that justifies estrangement or formal boundaries. This is not a pastoral response to genuine abuse; it is a framework that dissolves the fifth commandment by reinterpreting all parental authority through the lens of the child's autonomy. The Bible does not command honor only toward perfect parents.

A second corruption runs through the progressive state: the consistent legislative and cultural movement to transfer authority over children from parents to schools, courts, social services, and medical professionals — often explicitly framing parental conviction as a risk to be managed. The child who belongs to the state is a child who has been removed from the fifth commandment. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that family, church, and state are three distinct, God-given spheres; the state that colonizes the family is not a protector but a usurper.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin filius/filia (son/daughter) + pietas (dutiful reverence, proper devotion); in Reformed moral theology, filial piety is the content of the fifth commandment applied to children of all ages in their duties toward parents.

expand to see more

Latin filius / filia — son / daughter; the relationship of natural generation and covenant nurture that creates the duty.

Latin pietas — dutiful reverence, proper devotion; in classical Rome, the virtue of right relation to gods, parents, and country; Christianity reoriented it toward the one true God and His created order.

Hebrew kabbed (from kabad) — to give weight to, to treat as heavy; honoring parents means treating them as weighty — substantial, authoritative, deserving of gravity and respect.

Greek timaô / timê — to honor, to assign value; Paul's word in Eph 6:2, echoing the LXX of Ex 20:12, carries the sense of active valuation — treating the parent as one of high worth.

Hebrew ya'arikun yamekha — that your days may be long; the promised consequence locates filial piety in the covenantal economy, making honor of parents a matter of public, covenantal order.

Usage

"Filial piety is not slavish obedience above all else — it is properly ordered honor that remains under God (Acts 5:29), which means a child is not obligated to follow parents into sin."

"The fifth commandment's promise — length of days in the land — is both national (applied to Israel in Canaan) and typological (pointing to the inheritance of eternal life in the new creation for those who walk in God's order)."

"The first commandment with a promise is not the easiest commandment; in an age of expressive individualism, it may be one of the hardest — which is exactly why it needs to be preached."
